text:
Decades of remarkable progress against poverty and inequality have given way to a period of slower and more uneven gains. Between 1990 and 2020, the share of the world's population living in extreme poverty fell from 43 percent to 11 percent, driven largely by gains in large middle-income economies. The number of economies with high inequality, measured by a Gini index above 40, declined from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024. But progress has slowed, and extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in a few economies, most of them in Sub-Saharan Africa and in fragile and conflict-affected situations.

In 2026, an estimated 811 million people, 1 in 10, live below the international extreme poverty line of $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Without faster growth, the number will rise as populations grow more quickly where poverty is highest.

Escaping extreme poverty does not guarantee economic security. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, live below the $8.30-a-day poverty line typically used to measure poverty in upper-middle-income countries, leaving many vulnerable to falling back into extreme poverty after a shock. Weather-related shocks add to this vulnerability: 1.5 billion people, most living above the extreme poverty line, are exposed to climate hazards but lack the means to cope with these hazards. At the same time, the growth needed to end extreme poverty in the poorest countries would add little to global emissions.

This edition has a thematic focus on jobs, which the World Bank Group has made central to its development agenda toward a world free of poverty on a livable planet. Drawing on new data for more than 130 economies, it provides the first global profile of the work done by poor and nonpoor adults.

Jobs are the most direct pathway out of poverty for most households. Poor and nonpoor adults have similar employment rates. One in three adults in poor households are not employed, many of whom are women. Poor workers not only earn less, they also support more dependents. This means that reducing poverty requires both more jobs and better-paying jobs. Expanding employment can make the greatest difference for households living between the $3.00 and $8.30 poverty lines, while raising the earnings of poor workers can have the greatest impact on the poorest households.

text:
How to achieve this differs across countries. Where farms and household enterprises account for most jobs, raising productivity must go hand in hand with creating opportunities for wage employment. Where wage employment is established, access to better-paying jobs can lift households out of poverty. Jobs also help families that have escaped poverty withstand shocks and avoid falling back and, with this help, build a stronger middle class.

Reducing poverty requires both expanding opportunities to earn a living and increasing the returns to the work poor people already do. By bringing together new evidence on poverty, inequality, climate risks, and jobs, this report seeks to help chart a path toward renewed progress in ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet. Building on a decade of evidence and analysis, it seeks to help turn this knowledge into lasting progress.

Miki Khanh Doan is an Economist in the Distributional Impact of Policies Unit at the World Bank. Her work uses household data and applied microeconomic methods to examine how policies and shocks affect poverty, welfare, and resilience. At the World Bank, she focuses on the distributional impacts of climate shocks, agricultural policy, and climate-resilient development. Her broader research covers rural livelihoods, intrahousehold dynamics, food security, and human capital programs. Miki holds a PhD in agricultural and resource economics from the University of California, Davis, and a BA from the University of Richmond.

Ebad Ebadi is an Economist in the Development Research Group at the World Bank. His research examines the intersection of development, environmental, and labor economics, with a focus on sustainable growth and labor market outcomes. His work examines topics such as environmental degradation, climate change, jobs, and the distributional impacts of environmental and climate policies. Through empirical analysis, his research aims to generate evidence that informs policies promoting sustainable and inclusive development; bridges research and policy; and contributes to debates on environmental sustainability, labor markets, and economic development. Ebad holds a PhD in economics from George Washington University and an MS in economics from the London School of Economics and Political Science.

David Groves is a Lead Climate Change Specialist in the Chief Economic Advisor Unit of the Climate Department at the World Bank, where he manages the Climate Support Facility's Country Climate Strategies Program, helping countries develop and operationalize long-term, low-emissions development strategies. He also co-leads the Country Climate and Development Reports Program. Before joining the World Bank in 2021, he was a Senior Policy Researcher at the RAND Corporation, where he codirected the Climate Resilience Center and the Center for Decision Making Under Uncertainty. David holds a PhD in policy analysis from the Pardee RAND Graduate School, an MS in atmospheric sciences from the University of Washington, and an MS in earth systems from Stanford University.

Christoph Lakner is a Program Manager in the Development Data Group at the World Bank. He leads the Global Poverty and Inequality Data team, which manages the Poverty and Inequality Platform, the home of the World Bank's global poverty numbers. His research interests include poverty and inequality measurement, especially from a global perspective. Christoph holds a DPhil, a MPhil, and a BA in economics from the University of Oxford.

Poverty

1. The decline in extreme poverty has stalled. In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, are living on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Had the 2000-13 pace been maintained, 243 million additional people would have escaped poverty. The stagnation is confined to the extreme line; at $4.20 and $8.30, poverty reduction has kept the earlier pace (refer to figure 1, panel a).

2. Extreme poverty is concentrated, and demographic patterns will concentrate it further. More than half the extreme poor are living in nine economies, and, by 2030, 87 percent will be living in Sub-Saharan Africa, in a fragile and conflict-affected situation, or both (refer to figure 1, panel b). The population is growing most quickly where poverty rates are the highest; so, at the 2015-24 pace of economic growth, the global rate and the number of the extreme poor will be higher in 2030 than today.

3. Escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching the middle class. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, is still living on less than $8.30 a day, the poverty line in upper-middle- income economies. Most people who have left extreme poverty since 2000 have moved only into the $3.00-$8.30 band: no longer extremely poor, but not economically secure, and one shock away from falling back into extreme poverty. The size of the global middle class-people living on between $8.30 a day and the $28.00 prosperity standard-has roughly doubled as a share of the world's population over the same period, but its expansion has been concentrated in today's upper-middle-income economies, where the middle class is now the majority. In lower-middle-income economies, the vulnerable group living on between $3.00 and $8.30 a day is still the largest, and, in low-income economies, the middle class remains a small minority (refer to figure 1, panel c).

Prosperity

4. High inequality is retreating across economies but persists across people. The number of economies with a Gini index above 40 fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, and those economies still above the threshold cut their average Gini from 51 to 46. Nonetheless, one in five people worldwide is still living in a high-inequality economy, a share unchanged since 2013 (refer to figure 2, panel a), and 37 economies have never left the above-40 group in 25 years. The concentration of the extreme poor is happening here, too. The share in high-inequality economies nearly doubled, to 36 percent.

5. The Prosperity Gap halved and then stalled. In 1990, incomes worldwide needed to rise 10.5-fold, on average, to reach the $28.00-a-person-a-day prosperity standard. By 2013, the Prosperity Gap had fallen to 5.5, and it stood at 4.5 in 2026 (refer to figure 2, panel b, left panel). Almost all the progress occurred before 2013. Over the latest decade, the gap has narrowed by only about 1.2 percent a year (refer to figure 2, panel b, right panel). The gap in Sub-Saharan Africa is at 11.1, twice the global average and roughly where the world stood in 1990.

Planet

6. Climate risk reaches well beyond the poor. Of the 4.6 billion people exposed to a major climate hazard, 1.5 billion are also highly vulnerable because they lack social protection or access to basic infrastructure, and most of the highly vulnerable live above the extreme poverty line. The risk is concentrated in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan and the Sub-Saharan Africa regions, where nearly half and over a third of the population, respectively, are at high risk, and almost everyone who is exposed is also vulnerable. In South Asia, by contrast, the share of the population at risk has been brought below 20 percent by reducing vulnerability (refer to figure 3, panel a). Globally, the share of people at high risk fell from one in three in 2010 to one in six in 2024, although the number of people exposed rose by about 550 million.

8. Labor is the main and often only asset of the poor, but their work yields less income per household member than the work of the nonpoor. 9. More jobs and better-paying jobs both reduce poverty, but they reach different people. Raising employment in poor households to 75 percent, the rate poor men already attain, cuts extreme poverty by a fifth; raising education to the nonpoor average cuts extreme poverty by nearly half; and switching poor workers into nonagricultural employment or into wage work cuts it by a quarter to a third. All these simulations reduce the depth of poverty as well (refer to figure 4, panel c). The gains from better pay accrue mainly to the poorest. The gains from more work accrue mainly to the near-poor, among whom the nonworking adults are mostly women.

10. Poverty falls as the work of the poor becomes more productive, and, in the poorest economies, the work is mostly on farms and in household enterprises, not in wage jobs. In richer economies, households that move into wage employment are much more likely to escape poverty, while those that move into self-employment are not. In the poorest economies, the gain from wage employment is about a third as large, and the gain from self-employment, on the farm or off the farm, is not far below (refer to figure 4, panel d). The lowest rung of the ladder out of poverty is work on the farm, where higher yields raise earnings. Each step up represents a higher-productivity activity. The reach of the ladder is limited only by the ability of firms on the upper rungs to create jobs. So far, in the poorest countries, most of the movement upward has ended in microenterprise or self-employment activities rather than higher-earning wage jobs. Jobs matter in a second way as well: They keep households from falling back into poverty. It is this protection that transforms the exits from extreme poverty into a growing middle class.

At the same time, this report has three new elements worth highlighting. First, it presents new data. This report opens with a sobering projection. If economies grow over the coming years at the per capita economic growth rates experienced from 2015 to 2024, both the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will be higher in 2030 than today. This would not represent a mere pause, but a stunning reversal of the improvement in well-being of the preceding decades. Only sustained annual global economic growth of around 4 percent per capita would bring the global extreme poverty rate down to near the 3 percent target by 2050. However, this rate would be double the average country growth rate observed over the past 25 years.

The mechanism behind the projected reversal is linked to demographic trends (specifically population growth) and insufficient economic growth. Poverty rates in most high-poverty economies are projected to decline, though only marginally. The weight of these economies as a share of the world's population is expected to rise. The population is growing most quickly precisely in the locations that exhibit the highest poverty rates and that also often face conflict, fragility, and climate vulnerability. Thus, the global extreme poverty rate would be pulled upward even as the extreme poverty rates in most economies would hold steady or improve. The distinction matters for policy: The challenge is not a diffuse global failure of development, but the clustering of clear needs in an identifiable group of economies.

The places where extreme poverty persists are also increasingly places characterized by high inequality. One in five people in the world are living in economies classified as highly unequal. Among the world's extreme poor, the share is two in five, and this share has nearly doubled since 2000. The overlap compounds the challenge because high inequality weakens the poverty- reducing power of growth: The same rate of economic growth produces less poverty reduction in highly unequal economies.

The report's count of high-inequality economies illustrates what a headline figure may conceal. The count fell from 70 in 2000 to 42 in 2024, a decline of more than one-third. Underlying this trend, the report's fresh duration analysis reveals two findings that emphasize the stubborn persistence of inequality. In 2000-24, the Gini index never rose above 40 in 79 economies and never fell below 40 in 37 economies. The middle is thin. Few economies spent between 5 and 20 years above the threshold before falling below the threshold. High inequality is apparently not a transitory state through which economies pass. It is a chronic condition either avoided or endured for decades. The fall in the count of high-inequality economies should thus not be read as evidence that escape from high-inequality status is easy.

More encouraging is the fact that, among the 37 economies in which high inequality has endured, the average Gini index has declined from about 51 to about 46, and the decline has been broad across the distribution. Roughly a quarter of these economies now stand within three points of the threshold of 40. Transitions from high to moderate inequality are rare, but the progress that precedes an exit from high inequality accumulates across years before it is registered in a headline figure. Read together, these two findings demonstrate that it is more difficult to exit a situation of high inequality than the falling count suggests and that more exiting is under way than the count reveals.

The report's second prosperity indicator corroborates the diagnosis reached through the poverty data. The region's three most populous economies, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, account for 40 percent of the regional Prosperity Gap. All three are currently classified as fragile and conflict-affected states. Larger populations are only part of the story. Nigeria accounts for 18 percent of the population and 16 percent of the gap, and Ethiopia, for 10 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Yet, the Democratic Republic of Congo makes up 9 percent of the region's population, but accounts for 16 percent of its Prosperity Gap.

Measured across 103 economies, 17 percent of people are multidimensionally poor, that is, they are deprived in at least one of three dimensions (monetary welfare, education, and access to basic infrastructure), while 11 percent are deprived according to the monetary welfare dimension alone. This difference between multidimensional and monetary poverty is widest in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where it is driven by deprivations in education and sanitation.

The five planetary indicators tracked in this report reveal a further source of vulnerability. On balance, the situation is deteriorating: Greenhouse gas emissions are at record levels; ecosystems are shrinking; and food insecurity remains above prepandemic levels in many regions. Access to water and sanitation has improved steadily, and the share of people at high risk from climate hazards has fallen even as the absolute number of people facing such risk has grown. But progress is uneven; the gaps that remain are vast; and the pressures are affecting disproportionately the poor and those people who have only recently climbed out of poverty, thereby eroding the foundations on which durable poverty reduction depends.

Climate risk is an important direct channel through which a deteriorating planet impacts poor households. The report's climate risk indicator combines exposure to damaging climate hazards-such as flooding, drought, tropical cyclones, or extreme heat expected over a lifetime-with vulnerability, that is, a lack of capacity to cope if a hazard strikes. The vulnerability can be physical (limited access to water and electricity or limited mobility) or economic (low income, little education, no social protection, no access to financial services). Around 4.6 billion people live in exposed areas, and 2.7 billion live in highly vulnerable conditions; about 1.5 billion people experience both types of vulnerability. The drivers of multidimensional poverty also drive climate vulnerability. The same lack of schooling and missing infrastructure that identify a household as multidimensionally poor can convert a flood or a drought from a hazard into a catastrophe.

recorded the traits in the global profile of the poor, such as rural residence, low educational attainment, and the high share of children in the household, but has not detailed the link to jobs. This shortcoming has been caused by the lack of a sufficient database combining information on poverty and information on jobs at a global scale. This report has relied on the construction of such a database, which covers 96 percent of the world's population. The jobs profile complements the familiar profile of the traits of poverty.

Rural poverty is associated with agricultural work. Two-thirds of extremely poor workers are in farm jobs and are among the most exposed to climate variability and ecosystem stress. The education deficit becomes an earnings deficit among these workers. Poor workers earn little because the skills and knowledge they have are poorly matched to the demands of higher- paying labor markets. The demographic profile illustrates a dependency burden. A working adult in a poor household supports roughly three times as many dependents as a working adult in a rich household. The missing second earner in poor households is most often a woman. Employment among women is lowest globally among households in the lower middle of the distribution. Low female labor market participation is a structural driver of household poverty.

Labor income is the product of two factors: the amount of work a household supplies and the amount of earnings people receive if they work. This report examines poverty through each of these factors. It finds that neither factor alone accounts for the persistence of poverty and that addressing only one of these factors is insufficient to end poverty.

On employment rates, the poor fall only slightly short of the nonpoor. About three in five working-age adults in poor households are employed, some 6 percentage points below the rate among adults in nonpoor households. Joblessness thus accounts for only part of global poverty. The near parity in employment rates is a global average. The employment gap between the poor and the nonpoor is small or absent in poorer economies and wide in richer economies. It also conceals two shortfalls. Poor workers put in about three to four fewer hours a week relative to nonpoor workers, whether wage earners or self-employed, and the gap is largest in the poorest countries and among the self-employed. So, more work means not only a job but sufficient hours in the job. In poor households, the shortfall in employment is concentrated among women. Men are employed at rates of about 75 percent; women at far lower rates.

Over the past two decades, the gap between the poor and the nonpoor has widened. From 2003 to 2024, employment rates among the poor fell in 88 of 138 countries, and, in 99 of 137 countries, they grew more slowly or fell more quickly than the rates among the nonpoor at the $8.30-a-person-a-day poverty line (in 2021 purchasing power parity terms). Longer schooling among the young does not account for the decline, which is present among adults ages 25-64 as well. This report points to three mechanisms that it does not test directly. First, agriculture has shed workers more quickly than other sectors have absorbed them, and the poor, concentrated in agriculture, have been the first to be affected. Second, technical change may have lowered the demand for less well educated workers. Third, women leaving agriculture face constraints in taking up other work, ranging from care responsibilities and social norms to transport. Among the poor, the exit from farming may more often therefore end in nonemployment.

Combining both employment rates and earnings, this report shows that, over these two decades, growth in earnings per worker accounted for essentially all the welfare growth among the poorest households, while declines in employment rates reduced welfare growth. Poverty continued to decline as long as the growth in earnings more than offset the shrinking employment rate among the poor. The past two decades thus represent a missed opportunity rather than a verdict on employment. Had the level of employment among the poor been maintained, the same earnings growth would have reduced poverty more quickly.

How much can more jobs and better-paying jobs contribute to poverty reduction? Simulations undertaken for this report show that raising the employment rate among poor households to a benchmark of 75 percent of working-age adults would reduce the global poverty rate by a fifth. This is roughly the employment rate already observed among men in poor households, among poor households two decades ago, and in the richest quintile of the global population. Reaching this rate would therefore require closing much of the gender gap in employment because nearly all the shortfall is among women. Raising the earnings associated with the jobs held by the poor would reduce poverty further. Lifting the educational attainment of poor workers to the nonpoor average would cut the extreme poverty rate by nearly half. Labor movements out of agriculture and out of self-employment into wage work would contribute additional rate reductions.

In these simulations, the additional employment and the higher earnings reach different populations. The earnings gains are proportionally greatest among the poorest. The simulations assign broadly similar absolute gains to workers with similar characteristics, and, so, the gain is proportionally largest among the poorest workers. Meanwhile, the employment gains are concentrated among the near-poor, among whom the nonworking adults are disproportionately women. Better pay or higher returns to work (such as among smallholders or microenterprises) benefits the destitute the most. More work benefits the near-poor the most.

What has happened over the past two decades shows why these limits matter. The contraction of subsistence farming has fed mostly into nonagricultural forms of microenterprise or self- employment, mostly in services, rather than into higher-paying wage work. This represents a pattern of incomplete structural transformation. The distinction matters because a given rate of growth reduces poverty more quickly if it is accompanied by a movement of workers and earnings out of low-return agriculture than if the sectoral composition of the movement is neutral. Whether the poor can reach better-paying work depends on two factors: whether such work is created and whether workers have the skills and qualifications employers in higher- paying work require. Raising the productivity of the work the poor already do, especially on smallholder farms, is a route that does not depend on the creation of such jobs, and it is the route with the shortest horizon.

The simulations are not the only evidence. Additional evidence is supplied by household surveys that track job transitions into wage jobs and self-employment, out of farming, or into or out of work altogether and that track whether households escaped poverty or fell into poverty during the same years. Longitudinal surveys in 41 economies confirm that both more work and better-paying work are associated with poverty reduction. However, the job transitions that drive this result vary. A transition into a wage job is associated with poverty reduction in richer economies, while a transition out of agriculture into nonagricultural work of any kind matters most in poorer economies. If the share of a poor household's working-age members in wage employment rises by 10 percentage points, the household's chance of escaping poverty increases by 2.4 percentage points in upper-middle-income economies and by 2.2 percentage points in high-income economies, but by only 0.8 percentage points in low- and lower-middle-income economies. A shift into nonwage work raises the chance of escaping poverty by 0.5 percentage points in the poorest economies, not far below the corresponding effect of wage employment in these same economies, while the estimate is not distinguishable from zero in upper-middle- income economies and negative in high-income economies. Poor households in the poorest economies are held back twice over. The wage work within their reach may not generate the income necessary to lift these households out of poverty, as these estimates show, and such work is also scarce. Over the period under observation, the share of working-age adults in wage employment rose by 3.4 percentage points among poor households in the poorest economies, against 7.7 percentage points in high-income economies. Access to a job and access to decent pay are both needed, and, in the poorest economies, both are in short supply.

The longitudinal data also show that, in addition to lifting households out of poverty, employment helps keep households from sliding into poverty, though not always through the same type of work. Self-employment in agriculture and outside agriculture protects households against falling into poverty in rich and poor economies alike.

text:
The findings of this report support neither complacency nor despair. Most of the world has left extreme poverty behind, and the poverty that remains is concentrated geographically, socially, and across the dimensions of deprivation. Concentration establishes where the remaining poverty is located and who suffers from this poverty. Designing policies to reduce poverty depends on understanding both dimensions. The task will not be easy. This report documents that poverty is concentrated among the countries and the households that have been the hardest to reach; in fragile states; in regions vulnerable to climate risks; and in families with low education, low skills, and many dependents.

The challenge of concentrated poverty cannot be separated from the condition of the planet on which the poor live. The coming decades will bring continued warming, mounting pressure on ecosystems, and growing food and water stress. At the same time, poverty reduction must accelerate. Investments in climate resilience can therefore also be investments in poverty reduction. Protecting ecosystems helps preserve the natural asset base on which many poor households depend. Limiting the peaks and duration of warming reduces the risks borne disproportionately by people who have contributed the least to the problem and possess the fewest resources to cope.

Each route out of poverty examined above-employment restored to a level the poor attained two decades ago, schooling raised to the level the nonpoor already have, shifts into better- paying jobs, and the economic growth needed for all three-can be quantified: how much poverty each would remove and which poor households each would reach. Such change rarely occurs quickly. Education among the poor typically yields impacts only after the poor cohorts successfully complete the transition from school to work. The barriers are great. Employment rates among the poor, especially poor women, are stagnant or falling. In some regions, a sizable share of the population remains vulnerable to climate hazards. Inequality is often persistent. Still, progress is possible even under such challenging circumstances, as demonstrated by the improvements in well-being over the last three decades. The broad focus of this report, to monitor this progress, is not meant to be a passive record of slowly moving numbers, but a road map that keeps the conditions and the opportunities for poverty reduction in view.

text:
Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026: Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication assesses global progress toward ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet. After three decades of historic gains, extreme poverty reduction has stalled. In 2026, an estimated 811 million people, 1 in 10 worldwide, are living on less than $3.00 a day, while nearly half of humanity is living on less than $8.30 a day. Poverty is increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and fragile and conflict-affected situations, where rapid population growth, insufficient economic growth, and exposure to various shocks make progress extremely difficult.

Through the deeply probing lens of poverty, prosperity, and planetary sustainability, the report finds that the number of economies with high inequality is falling. Yet, many people, including a growing share of the extreme poor, are still living in highly unequal economies. And progress in closing the Global Prosperity Gap-an indicator that combines the tracking of both progress in average income and improvements in equity-has also slowed. Climate hazards, ecosystem degradation, food insecurity, and inadequate water and sanitation are threatening the gains in development, especially among those people and households with the fewest resources to withstand and recover from shocks. Ending extreme poverty would add relatively little to the cost or impacts of global emissions, demonstrating that poverty reduction and climate protection are not competing goals.

Placing jobs at the center, the report offers new evidence on how employment and earnings shape household welfare. Using survey data linking poverty with labor market outcomes, it offers a global profile of poor and nonpoor workers and examines pathways out of poverty through job opportunities. Poor people work nearly as much as the nonpoor but earn less, work fewer hours, and support more dependents. And one in three poor people have no employment. Both more jobs and better-paying jobs will reduce poverty, but the effects of each reach different groups. Increasing earnings matters most for the poorest, while increasing rates of employment, particularly among women, benefits the near-poor the most.

Poverty reduction requires that access to income-generating opportunities expands and that the returns to the work poor people already perform increase. This report-by tracking where poverty is concentrated, the progress on inequality, and the status of measures of a livable planet, combined with a unique profile of the work of the poor-seeks to inspire a data-driven agenda for reinvigorating global progress in these many dimensions.
